Title: Discuss the idea first
Body: You can bring an unfinished idea to the Advisor. Describe what interests you about the scene and explore it before handing a brief to the Writer.

Title: One question at a time
Body: If a scene has an unclear motive, setting, and ending, start with the biggest difficulty. A focused question makes the discussion easier to follow.

Title: Name your reader
Body: Tell the Advisor who you are writing for and what that reader already knows. This helps you discuss clarity without adding unnecessary explanations.

Title: The next scene's purpose
Body: Before discussing a scene, say what should change by its end: a relationship, knowledge, or the character's situation. This gives you a basis for evaluating suggestions.

Title: Constraints are useful
Body: State unwanted solutions early: a lucky rescue, a new character, or revealing a secret. Clear boundaries help the Advisor suggest ideas that fit your intentions.

Title: Name what is unknown
Body: If you have not chosen the reason for an action, say so. Ask to keep the question open so a working assumption does not appear settled.

Title: Mark accepted decisions
Body: After a discussion, state which option you chose and why. This helps distinguish your decision from other suggestions when preparing the Writer's brief.

Title: Ask for the reason
Body: Received a vague comment such as 'the character is unconvincing'? Ask the Advisor to identify the action and explain which reader expectation it conflicts with.

Title: Blue sends to Advisor
Body: The blue button sends text to the Advisor. In Writer mode, it returns to discussion; pressing it with an empty input returns without sending a new message.

Title: Red hands over the brief
Body: From the Advisor, the red button starts preparing the Writer's brief. Before pressing it, make sure the discussion clearly describes the next action you want written.

Title: What direct request means
Body: 'Direct request' hides the Advisor's brief preparation and starts the Writer immediately. Use it when your request is already specific enough to produce a paragraph.

Title: Read the brief first
Body: Turn off 'Direct request' if you want to read the brief first. Once it appears, the Writer starts when you separately choose 'Continue'.

Title: Refine the brief in discussion
Body: If the brief missed an important condition, return to the Advisor and describe the correction. Then hand the refined idea back to the Writer.

Title: Pair quotes with questions
Body: Attach a selected quote and explain what you want to discuss. For example, ask whether the transition from that line to the character's next action is clear.

Title: Remove an outdated quote
Body: Review attached quotes before sending. If your question has changed, remove an irrelevant quote so the assistant does not focus on the earlier passage.

Title: Check your keyboard recipient
Body: By default, Enter sends to the Advisor and Ctrl+Enter sends to the Writer. These assignments can change for each project, so follow your saved settings.

Title: New line without sending
Body: Shift+Enter adds a new line in the input. Use it to separate your request, constraints, and a short example before sending them to the assistant.

Title: Customize your send keys
Body: Right-click the role name or a send button to open settings. You can assign Enter and Ctrl+Enter to the actions you prefer for this project.

Title: History and current discussion
Body: A message marked 'Only in history' is not included in the next request as part of the conversation. Restate any condition that matters to a new discussion.

Title: A temporary free conversation
Body: 'Free chat' has no project context and does not save its conversation. Use the Advisor's project discussion when you need manuscript context and selected sources.

Title: One paragraph at a time
Body: The Writer is instructed to produce one paragraph. Break a large scene into the immediate action, the character's reaction, and the next turn.

Title: Choose what enters the manuscript
Body: The Writer's reply remains a proposal. Read it and transfer the text you want into the editor: you decide what becomes part of the manuscript.

Title: Continue from the editor
Body: Before using 'Continue', right-click it and check the basis. 'From editor' continues the current manuscript, including changes you made by hand.

Title: Continue from the reply
Body: 'From last reply' lets you develop the Writer's proposal before copying it into the manuscript. Check this choice so you continue the intended version.

Title: Give an observable detail
Body: For a new paragraph, name an object, movement, or sound that matters in the moment. A concrete detail helps express the mood through events.

Title: Set the paragraph's endpoint
Body: Say where to stop: before a character's answer, at the doorway, or after a brief reaction. This helps keep the paragraph within the intended moment.

Title: Specify the viewpoint
Body: Name whose viewpoint frames the scene. If other characters' thoughts are inaccessible, ask the Writer to convey them only through visible gestures and speech.

Title: Keep the narrative tense
Body: When starting a new passage, remind the Writer of the intended narrative tense. Check the reply for accidental shifts between present and past.

Title: Suggest an approximate length
Body: If you need a compact paragraph, suggest an approximate word count. Treat it as guidance for the Writer and assess the final length and readability yourself.

Title: Describe the character's voice
Body: Instead of asking for a 'distinctive voice', name a speech habit: short answers, cautious wording, or avoiding questions. Then check whether the dialogue sounds natural.

Title: State what must stay
Body: When revising a paragraph, list what must stay: who acts, what the character knows, and how the moment ends. This helps preserve its meaning.

Title: Check the target paragraph
Body: Revision actions apply to the Writer's current result. Before sending a comment, check that you mean the intended version, especially after several new replies.

Title: One revision at a time
Body: Revise the meaning first, then rhythm and wording. With fewer unrelated changes in one request, it is easier to see what changed and what stayed.

Title: Check the paragraph transition
Body: Before copying a reply, read it alongside the manuscript's ending. This makes repeated actions, sudden changes of place, or missing objects easier to spot.

Title: Copy a single reply
Body: 'Copy all' on a Writer reply copies that message alone. After pasting it into the manuscript, check that you have not left a duplicate paragraph.

Title: Add a condition before handover
Body: Before sending from the Advisor with the red button, you can leave a final clarification in the input. It is included alongside any unsent quotes.

Title: Stop an unwanted direction
Body: If you sent the wrong request, press 'Stop'. Clarify the task before sending again so you do not keep working from an unintended instruction.

Title: Wait for the current reply
Body: While the assistant is working, another send may be unavailable. Wait for the result or stop the request before choosing your next action.

Title: Your own instruction set
Body: The pencil in the top panel opens prompt sets. If you regularly repeat an instruction for the assistants, you can include it in your own copy.

Title: Return to standard prompts
Body: After changing your prompts, compare the behavior with the standard set. Built-in texts remain available, and an unusual reply may be related to your new instructions.

Title: An uncertain character choice
Body: Unsure why a character stays somewhere dangerous? Use 'Discuss' to explore their fear, desire, and available alternatives before writing the scene.

Title: Discuss the intended impression
Body: In 'Discuss', describe the feeling you want the scene to leave. Ask which elements support that impression and which pull it in another direction.

Title: Different causes of conflict
Body: Use 'Options' to request three causes for an argument: conflicting values, misunderstanding, and incompatible goals. Compare which cause best reveals your characters.

Title: Choose the cost of success
Body: Does the character's victory feel too easy? Use 'Options' to explore possible costs or consequences and choose those that fit your story.

Title: Compare scene openings
Body: Use 'Options' to consider opening with an action, observation, or short line of dialogue. Ask how each changes reader expectations before choosing.

Title: Clarify a vague request
Body: If your request is simply 'make it more interesting', choose 'Clarify'. Let the Advisor help identify whether it needs an obstacle, stakes, surprise, or a clearer goal.

Title: Clarify a hidden desire
Body: Use 'Clarify' to ask for questions about what the character wants from a conversation. Your answers can separate its apparent subject from their personal goal.

Title: Clarify a secret's boundaries
Body: Before a scene involving a secret, use 'Clarify'. Establish who knows the truth, who merely suspects it, and what readers may understand at this stage.

Title: Check what characters know
Body: Use 'Check' to look for moments where a character uses information they have not learned yet. Ask the Advisor to identify the line and possible gap.

Title: Check the chain of causes
Body: Use 'Check' to examine the link between an event and the character's decision. Ask where a reader might be missing a reason for the next action.

Title: Check a world rule
Body: If a character's ability solves an obstacle, use 'Check' to compare the episode with that ability's established costs and limits. Verify comments against the source.

Title: Find an earlier detail
Body: Forgot how you described a room? Use 'Find' with a specific question and ask for its source. Check that the relevant materials are selected.

Title: Find an earlier promise
Body: Before revisiting an old conflict, use 'Find' to locate the character's promise. Check the wording against its source before building a scene around it.

Title: Put the idea into words
Body: Use 'Phrase' with your scattered notes about a scene. Ask for a clear statement that preserves your constraints and questions you have not resolved.

Title: Phrase a precise revision
Body: In 'Phrase', explain what bothers you about the Writer's reply. Ask the Advisor to turn that impression into a clear instruction for the next revision.

Title: The character's next reaction
Body: After a surprising line, choose 'Continue' for the next paragraph. The brief can limit it to the character's reaction, leaving the other person's response for later.

Title: Move on without recap
Body: If 'Continue' repeats what was already shown, clarify the next new action with the Advisor. Hand over the updated brief and check the scene's continuity again.

Title: Another version of the moment
Body: Choose 'Regenerate' when the task is right but the execution does not work. It requests another version of the current paragraph using the same brief.

Title: Compare versions by purpose
Body: After 'Regenerate', compare versions against the scene's purpose: clearer action, a more convincing reaction, or better rhythm. The more unusual text is not necessarily the better fit.

Title: When regeneration does not help
Body: If several 'Regenerate' replies repeat the same problem, refine the brief itself. For example, explain what the reader should understand from this paragraph.

Title: A precise paragraph revision
Body: For 'Rewrite', name a specific change: 'Have the character refuse with a gesture, without answering directly.' Then check that the moment's other events remain intact.

Title: Revise an unnecessary explanation
Body: Use 'Rewrite' to replace an explanation of emotion with observable behavior. Specify which feeling matters and what the character is not yet saying aloud.

Title: Clarify where characters stand
Body: If it is unclear where everyone is, choose 'Rewrite' and describe the characters' positions. Ask for spatially clear actions while preserving the paragraph's events.

Title: Trim a repeated point
Body: Do two sentences make the same point? Try 'Shorter'. Then make sure an important reason for the character's action did not disappear with the repetition.

Title: Preserve a meaningful pause
Body: After 'Shorter', assess rhythm as well as length. A small pause before an answer may matter to the tension even if it could be removed.

Title: Stay in the current moment
Body: 'More detail' expands the same moment. Use it when a gesture or reaction passes too quickly and you are not ready for the next event.

Title: Check whether details help
Body: After 'More detail', keep details that reveal action, character, or setting. If description distracts from an important exchange, clarify what the passage should focus on.

Title: Expand the characters' interaction
Body: Try 'More detail' when a meeting is compressed into one general sentence. Check for observable reactions without an unrequested jump into a new scene.

Title: Name the intended tone
Body: With 'Tone', state the direction clearly: 'More restrained, without grand language; keep the events.' This is more precise than simply asking for more emotion.

Title: Tension without new events
Body: With 'Tone', ask for unease through the character's perception. Check the reply for new threats that were not part of your intended events.

Title: Inspect available sources
Body: Expand rows in 'Sources' to inspect the available information. A source's name alone does not mean it contains the answer to your question.

Title: Intent as a shared reference
Body: 'Calibrated project intent' supplies the work's general direction. Add specific guidance for an unusual scene so that the overall intent does not replace the immediate task.

Title: A concise plot anchor
Body: Keep stable guidance in a plot anchor, such as a world rule or the character's central limitation. A long list of incidental notes is harder to review.

Title: Two separate text collections
Body: The RAG editor separates reference material from the project's completed text. Check the section before editing: source-world information and your manuscript have different origins.

Title: Search returns passages
Body: RAG helps retrieve source passages for a request. Do not assume a selection replaces reading the whole book, especially when checking a long sequence of events.

Title: Edit the extracted text
Body: In the RAG editor's reference section, edits change extracted text while original files remain unchanged. Saving updates the index; check your correction in the intended section.

Title: A short exact quote
Body: If your question concerns one line of dialogue, attach that line instead of a long scene summary. An exact quote preserves important wording and negation.

Title: Name the relevant context
Body: When looking for a detail, name the nearby character, place, or event. A concrete situation gives more useful clues than asking 'what happened there?'

Title: Plans are not events
Body: The future route describes the author's intentions. When discussing existing text, distinguish steps that have happened from those that remain possible future developments.

Title: Check the current stage
Body: The current route stage does not switch automatically. Before a new scene, check the selected stage and align it with the manuscript's immediate task.

Title: Edit the route deliberately
Body: The route editor lets you change stage names and descriptions; new stages are added at the end. After editing, reread the transitions between neighboring stages.

Title: Summary and original scene
Body: A chapter summary helps you navigate. If a disagreement depends on exact dialogue, tone, or the order of actions, consult the scene itself.

Title: After editing a finished chapter
Body: Changing a finished chapter requires related information to be updated. The editor refreshes RAG after saving, and chapter memory is checked again when the window closes.

Title: Each role has an anchor
Body: The Advisor and Writer have separate plot anchors. If both need a constraint, check both anchors; clearing a chat does not remove them.

Title: Missing information is an answer
Body: If the assistant cannot find a detail in selected sources, do not treat a plausible guess as a discovery. Open the relevant material or clarify where to look.

Title: Draft and finished sections
Body: The editor's current text and finished chapters serve different roles. Before discussing an earlier scene, check where its current version is stored.

Title: Check a quote's origin
Body: The same wording may appear in the manuscript and an assistant's proposal. Before using a quote, check that it comes from the intended version.

Title: A fact needs review
Body: When adding information to Jelly, review each proposed record. Correct fields or deselect the record if the model has turned a guess into a statement.

Title: A quote must be exact
Body: A Jelly record needs a continuous quote from the source text. Even an accurate paraphrase does not replace the wording that supports the fact.

Title: Keep the negation
Body: When reviewing memory, pay attention to 'not', 'never', and conditions such as 'only if'. Losing one word can reverse a world rule or a character's promise.

Title: Who made the statement
Body: A character's words may be mistaken, dishonest, or someone else's opinion. When reviewing memory, distinguish narrative fact from a statement made within the scene.

Title: Intention and completed action
Body: 'Planned to leave' does not mean 'left'. Check memory records for plans, fears, or assumptions that have incorrectly become completed events.

Title: Memory does not rewrite text
Body: Editing a Jelly fact does not change the manuscript. If the scene also contains the error, revise its text separately and check the stored information again.

Title: Watch the save indicator
Body: After editing by hand, check the manuscript's save indicator. Before finishing a chapter or leaving the project, make sure the text has been saved.

Title: Read before finishing a chapter
Body: Before finishing a chapter, reread its opening, ending, names, and scene order. Expand the chapter controls near the editor's lower-right edge.

Title: Choose the original export
Body: Import accepts a native DeepSeek ZIP export or an extracted conversations JSON file. Start by selecting the original export and the future project's folder.

Title: Select the relevant conversations
Body: One export may contain several creative projects. Select the conversations relevant to the future book and review your selection before starting analysis.

Title: Highlighting helps you navigate
Body: A conversation with a similar title is highlighted as a hint. This does not automatically check its box: you decide which conversations to include.

Title: The first pass reads throughout
Body: The first pass analyzes all nontechnical parts of the selected conversations. An initial title guess is not used to narrow the search for literary text.

Title: Assemble the book with checkboxes
Body: After the first analysis, you can select multiple groups, title variants, and individual parts. This lets you include chapters found under different names in one book.

Title: Review the Other group
Body: Uncertain parts in 'Other' are initially included to help retain relevant text. Review them and deselect anything that clearly does not belong in the book.

Title: Similar titles need review
Body: Similar titles may refer to one book or different ideas. Use the composition review icon to inspect the source parts before including them together.

Title: Choose the contents first
Body: The book is not created before you choose its contents. Use this stage to review selected groups and check that an important chapter has not been left out.

Title: The second pass follows selection
Body: The second pass follows your selection, including uncertain parts you kept. Before assembling the book, check the boxes and your manual exclusions once more.

Title: Repeated analysis can differ
Body: Repeated analysis may produce different titles or assignments of parts. Compare the source passages rather than relying only on the number of groups found.

Title: An answer can stay blank
Body: During analysis, you can skip a text question and return to it. If you specified an existing reference source, its file step requires at least one file.

Title: Memory is a separate step
Body: The questionnaire's memory choice concerns later project work. In the current import flow, book review follows assembly; RAG and Jelly are not prepared yet.

Title: Keep the session folder
Body: Keep the session folder so you can resume an import. Its recent entry helps you return, while the resumable analysis data lives in the folder itself.

Title: The bin removes an entry
Body: The bin beside an unfinished creation removes its list entry. Project and import files remain on disk; this action does not clear the folder.

Title: The assembled book needs review
Body: Finished analysis means the result is ready for review. Read the book as a draft: the model may have chosen the wrong scene version or included commentary.

Title: Check the scene order
Body: After import, read the transitions between scenes. Watch the time, setting, and objects characters carry: these joins can reveal a missing or repeated passage.

Title: Compare uncertain versions
Body: If the export contains rewrites of a scene, check which version entered the book. A reply appearing later does not by itself prove that the author accepted it.

Title: Separate prose from discussion
Body: When reading the result, look for requests to the assistant, revision notes, and discussion of alternatives. These helped the conversation but need review in the book.

Title: Book and import history
Body: The DOCX is for reading the assembled book; the XLSX helps inspect import history. For a disputed passage, compare the result with source text and saved decisions.

Title: History includes personal text
Body: Import history contains original messages and model replies. Before sharing the XLSX with someone, inspect its contents: it may include more than the book itself.

Title: Describe a single image
Body: Image analysis can produce a literary description of one picture. First decide whether you need its setting, mood, or visible details for your next task.

Title: A batch of images
Body: A group of images can receive separate descriptions. Choose a combined document to review the batch or separate files for working with individual images.

Title: Choose a suitable mode
Body: Image analysis modes use different models and memory requirements. Choose an available mode suited to your computer; a heavier setup does not guarantee a better answer for every task.

Title: Stay close to the image
Body: For a factual description, choose the setting that keeps it strictly grounded in the image. Compare the answer with the picture; this setting does not eliminate errors.

Title: Separate accuracy and style
Body: In image analysis, first check that objects and actions are identified correctly. Judge the literary style after comparing the description with what is actually visible.

Title: Choose the description length
Body: A short description suits a quick image overview; a detailed one supports closer reading. Choose a length that fits your purpose without burying it in unnecessary detail.

Title: Heading or continuous text
Body: Image descriptions can use a heading or continuous text. Consider whether you will read the result on its own or include it in a larger document.

Title: Add a specific preference
Body: In image-description preferences, add a clear request such as 'fewer metaphors'. One specific requirement is easier to assess than a general request for prettier text.

Title: Your own image prompt
Body: Choosing a custom prompt disables some ordinary description settings because your text replaces them. Check that the prompt actually includes the requirements you need.

Title: Read the full description
Body: Preview the full image description before exporting. Check the ending too: unsupported conclusions or unnecessary invented details may appear there.

Title: Request a focused new version
Body: If an image description does not fit, request a new version with specific guidance. For example, ask for a shorter opening and more attention to the setting.

Title: Export the description
Body: You can export an image description to DOCX. Open the saved document and check whether its heading and text are easy to read in the chosen layout.

Title: Listen to an available summary
Body: In image analysis, use available summary narration if listening suits you better. Speech features depend on the selected mode and the components you have prepared.

Title: Start with a small trial
Body: Sandbox remains experimental. Start with a small task whose expected result you can independently open, read, and check.

Title: Inspect the experiment's result
Body: In experimental Sandbox, assess the actual result as well as the completion message. Check that it answers your request and contains the information you needed.

Title: The author sets the direction
Body: LOPATA helps you discuss and revise text while you decide its meaning. A useful reply supports your intent, even if you keep only one line.

Title: Local work uses resources
Body: A local model runs on your computer and uses its memory. Match the task's scale to available resources, especially when other demanding applications are open.

Title: Context has limits
Body: The assistant responds from available context, not your entire creative experience. If an important reason exists only in the author's mind, put it into words.

Title: Clear results support evaluation
Body: Before sending a request, decide what you will assess: clear action, accurate detail, or consistent characterization. An explicit goal makes the result's usefulness easier to judge.

Title: Confidence is not evidence
Body: Fluent wording can conceal an error. If a reply affects a fact, timeline, or world rule, check its basis as well as its persuasive delivery.

Title: Know what an action does
Body: Before an action, check which text it applies to and what result you expect. A clear connection between request and result helps you stay in control.

Title: A small verifiable step
Body: A large creative task is easier to manage through small changes you can evaluate. After each step, decide whether the text is closer to the intended reader experience.

Title: Waiting time is not quality
Body: Processing time depends on workload, model, and computer. A slow reply still needs review, while a quick response is not automatically a shallow one.

Title: A draft helps you choose
Body: Not every proposed paragraph needs to enter the book. Sometimes its value is helping you recognize the turn, rhythm, or image you actually want.

Title: Explain your criterion
Body: If a reply does not work, name the feature: overexplaining, excessive grandeur, or unnatural speech. A specific criterion turns your impression into useful guidance.

Title: Use ordinary language
Body: You do not need specialist terms to work with the assistants. Describe in ordinary language what should change in the text and what needs to stay.

Title: What the name means
Body: LOPATA means 'Local Offline Platform for AI Tools and Assistants'. Its name brings tools together around your work; it still helps to state the specific task clearly.

Title: Local work and internet access
Body: Prepared local models perform their work on your computer. Getting components, updates, and network tools may require internet access, so consider this when planning.

Title: Keep your own voice
Body: Perfectly smooth prose can lose your voice. Judge the assistant's suggestions against your own style: a distinctive rough edge can matter more than conventional polish.

Title: A finding and an idea
Body: A source finding and a new idea have different standing. Before accepting a suggestion, distinguish what is already in the book from what is being proposed.

Title: Keep access to the source
Body: Keep the original version when reworking substantial material. Being able to return to it helps you compare decisions and recover details that later prove important.

Title: Separate plans from available features
Body: An idea in a development plan is not yet an available feature. Use the current mode's capabilities and explanations when choosing how to complete your task.

Title: Choose tools for the task
Body: Image description and manuscript work serve different purposes. Identify the result you need first, then choose a mode and a way to assess its usefulness.

Title: Unusual choices can work
Body: An assistant's comment does not require you to follow convention. If an unusual choice creates the intended effect without accidental inconsistency, you can deliberately keep it.

Title: New context can change decisions
Body: A new author clarification can change how a scene should be judged. Explain what is now known so revisions respond to substance instead of endlessly repeating the same request.
